paper_title: Your LR Schedule May Not Be Principled: Effective Learning Rate Scheduling in Weight-Normalized Training

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Weight-normalized (WN) training is emerging as a compelling alternative to conventional weight decay (WD), with recent studies reporting substantial pretraining loss gains. We show that these gains are driven primarily by the induced effective learning rate (ELR) trajectory rather than by normalization alone. Matching ELR trajectories largely collapses the training loss dynamics of WN and WD. Schedule design should therefore target ELR rather than the nominal learning rate (LR) alone. Building on this principle, we propose AIR (Affine Inverse-square-Root decay), which combines a theoretically derived $1/\sqrt{t}$ decay with an affine adjustment to satisfy prescribed peak and terminal LRs over a finite training horizon. We further identify late-stage ELR scheduling as a key source of its gains, because a shared late schedule attenuates the effect of earlier LR choices. Experiments on 128 B-token Mixture-of-Experts pretraining demonstrate that AIR outperforms cosine and other candidate schedules in training loss, downstream performance, and hyperparameter robustness, reducing terminal training loss by approximately 0.01 relative to cosine at matched cumulative LR. Applying the same ELR trajectory to WD reproduces the corresponding training dynamics, showing that the benefits extend beyond fixed-norm training and establishing ELR as the principled scheduling object.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: In Large Language Model (LLM) pretraining, weight-normalized (WN) training [23, 33] has emerged as promising alternative to conventional weight decay (WD) [20]. It keeps parameter norms fixed after each update, with recent work reporting lower pretraining loss, improved token efficiency, greater stability, and better hyperparameter transfer [1, 18, 33]. Yet WN and WD exhibit markedly different training dynamics under the same learning rate (LR) schedule. As shown in Figure 1(a), under cosine decay [19], WN initially trails WD but eventually outperforms it. However, under warmup-stable-decay (WSD) [10], WN remains behind WD throughout training and ends with substantially higher loss. Therefore, understanding this contrast is essential to explaining when and why WN outperforms WD. We attribute this contrast to the effective learning rate (ELR) [5, 29], defined as ηeff = η/r, where η is the 1 Figure 1 WN achieves lower final loss than WD under cosine, but significantly higher under WSD. Effective LR (nominal LR / all-parameter norm) is the key driver of loss dynamics. Figure 2 ELR matching collapses WD-WN training loss dynamics. Training loss minus the WD baseline under (a) cosine or (b) AIR, paired at the same step; zero denotes the reference. Arrows indicate the ELR target, matched by replaying WD norms (via norm) or rescaling blockwise LR (via LR). WDWN also replays WD norms. nominal LR and is the norm of parameter block. In our study, we discover that the loss dynamics is strongly related to the decay of ELR. When WN and WD share the same WSD LR schedule, their ELR is governed entirely by the parameter norm r, which evolves very differently in the two regimes (Figure 1(b,c)). WN fixes the parameter norm, holding its ELR constant at peak throughout the entire stable phase and leading to slow decrease in loss. By contrast, WDs ELR keeps falling steadily, owing to the continuing growth of its parameter norm. This sustained ELR decay keeps its loss dropping much faster than WN. more interesting finding is that the loss dynamics of WN and WD largely collapse onto common trajectory once we align their ELR trajectories, whether by replaying WDs norms or by rescaling ones blockwise LRs. Taken together, these findings lead us to our core conclusion: ELR is the key driver of the loss dynamics. WNs core advantage actually comes from better ELR schedule, not normalization alone. Principled LR schedule design should therefore target ELR rather than the nominal LR alone. This core idea naturally inspires an essential research question: What should better ELR schedule look like? To make this practical, we introduce AIR (Affine Inverse-square-Root decay), decay through an affine transformation to meet prescribed peak and terminal LRs which adapts this 1/ over finite horizon. further analysis shows how shared late-stage schedule attenuates the alignment differences induced by earlier LR choices. This helps explain our finding that late-stage ELR scheduling is key source of AIRs gains. 2 Empirically, we evaluate AIR against cosine decay and alternative LR schedule families. In 128 B-token Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) [25] pretraining, AIR reduces terminal training loss by approximately 0.01 relative to cosine decay. Among these families, it achieves the lowest loss, the best downstream performance, and the greatest robustness to hyperparameter choices. Consistent with our theoretical analysis, controlled experiments show that the final training loss gaps between schedules narrow substantially when they share the same late-stage AIR schedule and differ only in their earlier LR trajectories. Transferring the induced ELR trajectory to WD also reproduces the corresponding training dynamics, showing that the benefits extend beyond fixed-norm training. In summary, our contributions are: We identify the induced ELR trajectory as the key driver of WNs loss advantage over WD. Matching ELR trajectories largely aligns their training loss dynamics, highlighting ELR, rather than nominal LR alone, as the target for schedule design. We propose AIR, an affine 1/ schedule for finite-horizon pretraining. Its decay shape follows from theoretical analysis of directional alignment under WN, which also helps explain the role of late-stage ELR scheduling in AIRs gains. We empirically validate AIR against cosine decay and alternative schedule families in 128 B-token MoE pretraining, demonstrating improvements in training loss, downstream performance, and hyperparameter robustness. It reduces terminal training loss by approximately 0.01 relative to cosine at matched cumulative LR. Applying the same ELR trajectory to WD reproduces the corresponding training loss dynamics.

Experimental setup. Under the same matched controls, we sweep each family’s shape parameter, which also

sections.content: Results. Figure 4 plots terminal training loss against peak LR with family-wise polynomial fits, and Table 5 in Appendix C.5 reports the resulting LR sensitivity. AIR has the lowest LR sensitivity over the widest range of peak LR. Its region of low loss is therefore wide enough that the gain does not depend on narrowly tuned peak LR and thus facilitates LR transfer [21].

sections.title: 6 Related Work
sections.content: WN and related constraints provide explicit parameter-scale control as an alternative to WD, with reported efficiency and stability gains [1, 33]. Methods differ in whether they separate magnitude from direction [23] or fix weight and update norms [33]. The choice of matrix norm further shapes the weight constraints and update geometry [35, 36]. For manifold constraints, Su [26, 27] and Bernstein [2] optimize tangent-space descent directions before retracting weights, so that the update respects the imposed geometry. Beyond norm control, scheduling determines how the effective step size evolves during training. River-valley analyses explain WSD [32], while convex bounds and functional scaling laws motivate cooldown and power decay [14, 24]. However, these theories focus on nominal LR alone, which is not principled when parameter norms evolve [5]. Concurrent work corroborates our finding that matching ELR largely aligns WN and WD 9 loss dynamics [17, 34, 38], but does not derive decay law from an optimization objective. We address this gap by optimizing directional alignment under WN to derive 1/ decay, then adapting it to finite horizons through an affine transformation, yielding AIR as an effective ELR schedule.

sections.title: 7 Conclusion and Future Work
sections.content: We identify the induced effective learning rate (ELR) trajectory as the key driver of WNs advantage over WD, with matched ELRs largely aligning their training loss dynamics. This finding motivates schedule design that targets ELR directly. Our theoretical analysis of directional alignment under WN, together with an affine adaptation of the unconstrained optimal 1/ schedule, yields AIR for finite-horizon training. Experiments on MoE models at two scales show that, at matched cumulative LR, AIR reduces terminal loss by about 0.01 relative to cosine and improves downstream performance, while schedule sweeps demonstrate hyperparameter robustness. Further stage-wise interventions show that sharing the late schedule substantially narrows final loss gaps from different early schedules, identifying late-stage scheduling as key source of AIRs effectiveness. Transferring its ELR trajectory to WD reproduces WN training loss dynamics, demonstrating that our design extends beyond fixed-norm training. Future work includes extending our directional-alignment theory to account for evolving update statistics and quantitatively connect alignment to loss. We also aim to investigate the ELR principle and AIR across more architectures, optimizers, and larger training scales, and to study ELR scheduling in continued training (CT), supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and reinforcement learning (RL).
